question.stem:
A machine learning engineer is preparing a dataset to fine-tune a multimodal Gemini 3 model using supervised fine-tuning for an automated visual inspection application. Each training example contains two images: an overview shot of an assembly item and a high-resolution close-up photo of a potential micro-defect. 

The engineer has the following requirements:
 Maximize the model's perception of fine detail in the micro-defect close-up.
 Minimize token consumption for the overview shot to optimize training efficiency and cost.
Comply with documented Google Cloud constraints for Gemini image tuning datasets.

How should the engineer prepare and configure the supervised fine-tuning dataset?
question.correct_answer: In the training dataset, set part-level mediaResolution to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH on the close-up image part, and configure the global mediaResolution in generationConfig to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW. Ensure each image file size does not exceed 20 MB and that no example exceeds 30 images.
question.correct_explanation: Key constraints from the stem: Maximize detail on the close-up defect image. Minimize token consumption for the overview image. Adhere to Gemini image fine-tuning dataset limits and schemas. How the correct answer addresses these constraints: In Gemini 3 and higher, you can set the media resolution per individual media Part, allowing you to mix resolutions across different images in a single example. Part-level media resolution settings take precedence over global settings. Setting mediaResolution to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW globally in generationConfig sets the overview image to 64 tokens, while applying MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH at the part level ensures the defect close-up receives full detailed token representation (256 tokens plus pan-and-scan tokens). Google Cloud documentation enforces specific image fine-tuning limits: a maximum image file size of 20 MB and a maximum of 30 images per example. Why alternatives fail: Distractor 1 fails because Gemini fine-tuning natively supports up to 30 images per example, making it unnecessary and incorrect to split multi-image examples due to an imagined single-image limit. Distractor 2 fails because Gemini 3 explicitly supports part-level media resolution overrides, so settling for global MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW unnecessarily degrades close-up defect analysis. Distractor 3 fails because mediaResolution is explicitly supported in fine-tuning datasets and controls token representations without modifying the physical image dimensions.
question.distractor_1: In the training dataset, set global mediaResolution in generationConfig to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH and split the overview shot and the close-up defect photo into separate individual training examples, because Gemini supervised fine-tuning restricts datasets to a maximum of one image per example.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This violates the documented limits of Gemini image tuning datasets. Gemini supervised fine-tuning allows up to 30 images per example, so multi-image examples do not need to be separated into single-image examples.
question.distractor_2: In the training dataset, set global mediaResolution in generationConfig to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW across all parts, because Gemini fine-tuning schemas do not support part-level overrides and require uniform token resolution for all images in an example.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to maximize fine detail perception on the defect close-up. For Gemini 3 models and higher, Google Cloud explicitly supports setting mediaResolution per individual media Part, and part-level settings take precedence over global settings.
question.distractor_3: Physically resize and downsample the pixel dimensions of the overview images before storing them in Cloud Storage, because mediaResolution only alters physical image dimensions and is supported exclusively during online inference rather than supervised fine-tuning.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This is technically incorrect based on Gemini documentation. The mediaResolution setting controls the tradeoff between media file quality and token count without affecting the physical image dimensions sent to the model, and it is explicitly supported within the fine-tuning dataset schema (generationConfig and Part).

question.stem:
A machine learning engineer is preparing a supervised fine-tuning dataset for a Gemini 3 model to perform automated visual inspection of manufactured equipment. Each training example requires two images:
A primary close-up photo of a component where perceiving fine surface defects is critical.
A secondary wide-angle photo that only provides general contextual placement.

The engineer needs to maximize the model's perception of defect details on the close-up photo while minimizing overall token consumption across the dataset.

How should the engineer configure the dataset JSON structure?
question.correct_answer: Set mediaResolution to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW in the global generationConfig, and set mediaResolution to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH at the individual media Part level for the defect close-up image.
question.correct_explanation: 1) Key constraints from stem: The solution must tune a Gemini 3 model on multimodal data with two images per example. It must maximize detail perception for the primary defect photo while minimizing overall token consumption for the contextual photo. 2) How solution addresses each constraint: In Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, fine-tuning Gemini 3 models supports setting mediaResolution per individual media Part, which takes precedence over global settings. Setting the global generationConfig to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW ensures contextual images consume only 64 tokens, while setting MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH at the Part level for the close-up image allocates 256 tokens plus pan-and-scan tokens to capture fine details. 3) Reference specific services/features: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Gemini 3, generationConfig, mediaResolution, Part. 4) Why alternatives fail: Setting global MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH and resizing file dimensions does not reduce the token allocation per image. Splitting into separate examples is unnecessary and incorrect because Gemini image tuning supports up to 30 images per example. Claiming that part-level media resolution is ignored or unavailable contradicts documented Gemini 3 capabilities where part-level settings explicitly override global settings.
question.distractor_1: Set mediaResolution to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH globally in generationConfig, and resize the file pixel dimensions of the contextual overview images before storing them in Cloud Storage.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize token consumption. In Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, mediaResolution controls token allocation rather than source pixel dimensions; setting MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH globally applies high token usage across all images unless overridden by part-level configuration.
question.distractor_2: Split each training example into two independent training records containing only one image each, because Gemini supervised fine-tuning restricts input to a single image per example.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This violates the scenario constraint of presenting both images together and contradicts Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform image tuning limitations, which permit up to 30 images per training example.
question.distractor_3: Set mediaResolution to MEDIA_RESOLUTION_MEDIUM globally in generationConfig, because part-level media resolution configurations are ignored during Gemini supervised fine-tuning.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to maximize defect detail perception while minimizing contextual tokens, and it incorrectly claims part-level settings are ignored. For Gemini 3 and higher, part-level mediaResolution is fully supported and takes precedence over global configurations.

question.stem:
A machine learning engineer needs to evaluate and prototype a solution using an open-source foundation model discovered in Model Garden. The prototyping plan has the following requirements:
Perform initial prompt testing of the model's generative capabilities without deploying custom infrastructure or incurring prediction compute charges.
Use the curated model-specific fine-tuning tutorial notebook within Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Workbench to develop the prototype.
Execute the resource-intensive notebook training job on dedicated GPU hardware such that the job runs to completion even if the interactive Workbench instance is shut down to avoid idle compute costs.

Which approach should the engineer take?
question.correct_answer: Test the model using the Demo playground in the Try out panel on the Model Garden model card. Open the model's tutorial notebook in an Agent Platform Workbench instance, and use the Workbench executor to run the notebook file on Agent Platform custom training with the required GPU hardware.
question.correct_explanation: The scenario requires zero-cost initial testing, prototyping using Model Garden notebooks in Workbench, and running a compute-intensive notebook on dedicated GPU resources while allowing the interactive Workbench VM to remain shut down. Model Garden Demo playgrounds are powered by predeployed endpoints and do not incur charges, allowing users to quickly evaluate model text responses in the Try out panel. Model Garden provides model-specific tutorial notebooks that can be opened and developed directly within Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Workbench. The Agent Platform Workbench executor executes notebook files as one-time or scheduled jobs on Agent Platform custom training. It allows users to specify custom hardware (such as dedicated GPUs) and runs independently in the background, completing the job and saving output to Cloud Storage even when the Workbench instance is shut down. Alternative approaches fail because Model Garden Spaces deploy endpoints and Cloud Run instances that incur charges, deploying dedicated prediction endpoints incurs compute costs, and executing jobs directly on the Workbench VM fails when the instance shuts down.
question.distractor_1: Launch a Model Garden Space from the model card to perform initial prompt testing. Open the model's tutorial notebook in an Agent Platform Workbench instance, and execute the notebook cells interactively in JupyterLab with automated idle shutdown enabled.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the zero-cost requirement and execution persistence requirement. Model Garden Spaces deploys the model to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and deploys a Gradio web application on a Cloud Run instance, which incurs charges for both the prediction machines and the Cloud Run instance. Furthermore, running the notebook interactively in JupyterLab means that if the instance shuts down due to idle detection or manual shutdown, the execution is terminated.
question.distractor_2: Deploy the open-source model to a dedicated Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform online prediction endpoint from the model card to evaluate prompts. Open the model's tutorial notebook in an Agent Platform Workbench instance, and run the notebook as a background process on the underlying Compute Engine VM.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This violates the cost constraint and execution requirements. Deploying a model to an online prediction endpoint incurs charges for the deployed compute resources. In addition, running the notebook as a background process directly on the Workbench instance's underlying Compute Engine VM requires the VM to stay powered on; shutting down the instance to save idle costs will terminate the VM and halt the background run.
question.distractor_3: Submit fine-tuning prompt datasets directly through the Model Garden Demo playground to customize model weights without charges. Export the resulting model checkpoint to an Agent Platform Workbench instance to run the tutorial notebook.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This violates Model Garden functional capabilities. The Model Garden Demo playground is limited to text input and output only for testing predeployed model capabilities; it does not support model fine-tuning or custom dataset training. Fine-tuning must be executed using custom pipelines, custom training jobs, or notebook environments.
